title: Alaska election officials oppose Trump DOJ’s involvement in Senate race
content: Alaska officials said new revelations in The New York Times about efforts by Democrats to recruit a Senate candidate with the same name as GOP incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan do not change the state’s opposition to a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to potentially delay certification of the election. The Times story , a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law told CNN in an email, confirms the “initial concerns” election officials had about the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, but it has “no impact on the current litigation.” “Placing candidates on the ballot is a matter of state law, not federal law,” said spokesperson Sam Curtis, noting that the Alaska Supreme Court has already decided that Daniel J. Sullivan would be on the ballot. The Justice Department, meanwhile, is citing a federal law in the case that “does not dictate what candidates can run in elections and does not authorize the relief the DOJ seeks,” Curtis said. “The Division is bound by the Alaska Supreme Court’s order and is committed to running a fair election and assisting voters as needed,” Curtis said. The story published Wednesday rattled one of the country’s most competitive Senate races with less than a week until Election Day. Mary Peltola, the state’s former at-large House member, is considered one of Senate Democrats’ top recruits of the midterms and her campaign continues to deny any involvement in Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign. Republicans have been concerned enough about the race that both President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have made trips to Alaska in recent weeks. Trump, who has complained about the two Sullivan issue for months and said he directed the Justice Department lawsuit last week, piled on with multiple social media posts slamming Peltola over the story, including one that said she “should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted.” “So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Nothing else will do!” The incumbent’s campaign accused Peltola of spending months “gaslighting Alaskans.” “We always knew this was a concerted effort to deceive Alaskans, and Mary Peltola was hoping it would stay covered up until after the election,” the campaign spokesman for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, Nate Adams said in a statement. Attorney General Todd Blanche on Fox News touted the Times’ story as proof that the Justice Department was right in bringing its unprecedented federal lawsuit. But when pressed over whether anything illegal had occurred that gives the DOJ the ability to intervene in the election, which is run by states, Blanche could not say. The Justice Department on Wednesday told a federal judge it would like to seek answers and evidence from Peltola’s campaign regarding the Times report and Sullivan issue, which it called a “conspiracy.” Some Democrats noted that Republicans have also meddled in the race to boost spoiler candidates. An array of GOP groups, for example, contributed to a super PAC that attacked Peltola in the primary and promoted a lesser-known Democratic candidate and a Green Party candidate. “This is basically a more extreme version of what the parties do all the time, which is try to find a candidate on the other side who can siphon votes away from the major party competitor,” election law specialist Rick Hasen told CNN. “And, you know, you can’t really hold someone responsible for impure motives.” Dean Franita Tolson of the University of Southern California Gould School of Law said the Times reporting doesn’t give the Department of Justice’s lawsuit any more credence. “At the end of the day, the federal government should not try to block certification of a race because they don’t like the outcome,” she said. “It, I think, makes the Peltola campaign look bad,” Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame Law School, added. “I think it will adversely affect her in the eyes of some voters, but from litigation perspective, I think it really won’t affect things at this stage.”

title: Why Trump’s latest election warning is impossible to ignore
content: When President Donald Trump signals he might not accept the result of an election, he’s worth taking seriously. By now, in his fifth national election as Republican Party leader, Trump has an established MO. He spends months whipping up doubts about the voting system and the integrity of election officials while suggesting Democrats may cheat. Then, he weaponizes the vortex of mistrust he created and implies before votes are counted that the election may not be fair. A week from Election Day, it feels more like Groundhog Day. Trump was asked Tuesday if he will accept the midterm election results, which could mean a tough night for the GOP , “whatever happens.” This would hardly be a question for another other modern president. But Trump’s reply came with a caveat made all the more ominous by his past conduct: “I will, if they are honest elections, yeah.” There’s a lot to be worried about here, beyond the equivocation of his answer. That’s because Trump effectively presents himself as the sole referee of the probity of an election. When he lost the presidential election in 2020, he falsely claimed fraud, despite multiple Republican officials, courts and even his own Justice Department proving there were no such irregularities. Trump’s latest hedging over an election came in a threatening context. He’s spent much of this year trying to skew the midterms in the GOP’s favor by pushing a midterm gerrymandering effort in Texas and other states and by unsuccessfully demanding Congress pass a voter registration and ID law that critics say would disenfranchise millions of citizens. And he recently ordered the Justice Department to sue to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate election if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, even though the Constitution grants a president no power to administer elections. Trump insists that a separate candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan could confuse voters and that his candidacy is a Democratic conspiracy. Alaska’s Supreme Court has ruled the second Sullivan can legally run in the election. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Democrats affiliated with the campaign of the party’s Senate nominee, Mary Peltola, recruited the other Sullivan, a retired teacher, to run. Her campaign denies any involvement. Peltola has asked a judge to strike down the DOJ’s suit before Election Day. In another preemptive strike, the DOJ on Friday ordered California to identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls and set aside their mail-in ballots — warning that officials who knowingly count noncitizens’ ballots could face criminal liability. A federal appeals court blocked that DOJ gambit . But the administration’s maneuvering raises the possibility of a post-election showdown. And in contrast with 2020, when then-Attorney General Bill Barr rebuffed Trump’s accusations of expansive electoral fraud, the department seems less likely to contradict him this time. The scars of one of the darkest days in modern American history — January 6, 2021 — mean that Trump’s latest election maneuvering is particularly loaded. Months before MAGA supporters smashed their way into the US Capitol, some beating up police officers, Trump had been poisoning their confidence in the 2020 election with remarkably similar language to that he used on Tuesday. “I hope it’s going to be a fair election. If it’s a fair election … I am 100% on board,” Trump said in his first presidential debate against Joe Biden in September 2020. “But if I see tens of thousands of ballots being manipulated, I can’t go along with that.” Four years later, when Trump was asked by Dana Bash at a CNN presidential debate whether he would accept the result of the election regardless of who won, he replied: “If it’s a fair and legal and good election — absolutely.” Trump did not dispute the results in 2024. The reason is obvious: He won. Four years earlier he’d lost. Trump’s serial election denialism in the absence of any widespread US election fraud raises the question of why he, alone among presidents, can’t accept the democratic reality that sometimes you lose elections. One answer is that Trump has given plentiful evidence that he cares more about power than the principle that voters get to pick their leaders. Another is that Trump has built a personal brand as one of life’s ultimate winners. This brittle veneer is incompatible with any perception of being a loser — one reason he still can’t admit he lost to Biden in 2020. But what might he try to do if the election goes badly for Republicans this time? The DOJ’s intervention in Alaska implies a post-election legal campaign if Peltola tallies one of the four net gains that Democrats need for a Senate majority. Similar moves elsewhere cannot be ruled out. Republican elected officials and attorneys general in key states can expect to come under withering pressure from Trump, if his failed bid to force GOP officeholders in Georgia to “find” votes in the 2020 election is any guide. There’s now no Barr equivalent to debunk potential claims of fraud. Current Attorney General Todd Blanche said on NBC’s “Meet the Press” in August that he could not pledge the department would always act independently of Trump. On Sunday, Blanche said on CNN’s “State of the Union” the administration was doing nothing “improper” in Alaska and simply wanted to ensure the rightful person wins, saying, “President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape, or form.” But he vehemently rejected the idea that the president’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election justified any concerns about his remarks smearing the 2026 midterms: “It’s not a conversation about January 6.” In 2020, America’s legal and constitutional guardrails held firm. But Trump is now less encumbered by aides ready to temper his most antidemocratic instincts. Still, Democrats and state officials of both parties who oversee elections have had months to prepare for potential threats from White House officials and local MAGA operatives. If Democrats win big, Trump may have less latitude to interfere. If the result is closer, it is possible that prolonged legal battles could deadlock the fate of the Senate for weeks. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely House speaker if Democrats win a majority, last week told CNN’s Manu Raju he assumed Republicans would “try to come up with any diabolical scheme to prevent November 3rd from being a free and fair election.” And it’s not unprecedented for the seating of a new senator to be challenged, according to lawyer and elections expert Ben Ginsberg. “It is done really rarely. It rips apart the fabric of the institution of the Senate when it happens,” Ginsberg said on CNN’s special election coverage on Sunday. Trump could have powerful incentives to challenge unfavorable election results, since Democrats are already planning a relentless campaign of investigations into the White House, the Cabinet and the Trump family’s financial dealings. But would a lame-duck president with an approval rating in the 30s who’d just lost a major national election have the political juice to pull it off? And Trump’s self-absorbed campaign posture has indicated little concern for vulnerable Republicans. He may simply care less when his name isn’t on the ballot. The president seemed Tuesday to be at least contemplating a period of bitter cohabitation with a Democratic Congress. “Look, I have a strong veto. I hope that won’t be the case, but if it is, that has happened before with many presidents,” he said. But Trump often follows through on his threats. And his latest electoral caveating shows he still thinks an election he loses must be unfair. So it’s a good idea to take him at his word. This article has been updated with new reporting.

title: Trump administration kicks out Cuban diplomat from US as tensions rise
content: US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said the Trump administration is ejecting a Cuban diplomat from the United States amid soaring tensions between Washington and Havana. The ejection comes after a shouting match erupted on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly Hall between Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla during a session on the US economic embargo against Cuba. It also comes as administration officials have again increasingly raised the specter of US action on the island. Secretary of State Marco Rubio “signed the paperwork to eject the Cuban diplomat, the first secretary of their delegation,” Waltz said Tuesday evening. “He’s gone. He’s going to be on a plane to Havana within the next 24 hours,” Waltz said in an interview on Fox News. He accused the diplomat of shoving and trying to “assault one of our American diplomats.” Waltz reiterated in another Fox interview on Wednesday that the Cuban diplomat “will be on a flight back to Havana and out of this country today.” “You lay a hand on an American here in the United States, President Trump, Secretary Rubio, and myself, we’re not going to stand for it. There will be consequences,” Waltz said Tuesday. “We have made clear to the Cuba Mission that this individual is not welcome in the United States, and as a result this individual has left,” a State Department spokesperson told CNN Wednesday. “Members of the incompetent communist Cuban regime showed their true essence through their intimidation and oppression tactics. Those tactics will not work, nor will they be tolerated.” CNN has reached out the Cuban Mission to the UN for comment. Videos from the Tuesday show members of the Cuban delegation hitting a table and the foreign minister shouting for a point of order as Waltz spoke. Rodríguez Parrilla approached the podium, and the two began shouting over each other. “This individual needs to back away from this podium. He’s not going to intimidate me in the United States of America like he tries to intimidate political prisoners,” Waltz yelled from the podium. “I’m the representative of the United States of America. Back up!” Shouts calling Waltz a liar were heard. Another video shared by Waltz’s account on X showed a Cuban diplomat swatting away the phone taking the video, with that diplomat saying the person was violating their personal space. Later Tuesday, the Cuban Mission to the UN sent a letter to the Secretary General expressing deep concern about that incident. In the letter, the Cuban mission said a US diplomat had invaded the Cuban diplomat’s personal space to film them and put the videos on social media with the intention of damaging the Cuban diplomat’s reputation. On Wednesday, the UN General Assembly overwhelming passed a resolution condemning the longstanding US embargo against Cuba, 130 votes in favor, 17 against, and 25 abstentions. The Trump administration in recent months had ratcheted up economic pressure on Cuba as it sought to force changes to the Castro government. In recent days, however, they have also increased their public rhetoric about possible US intervention to oust the longtime government in Havana. On Friday, Rubio posted on X , “To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time.” ‘The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA,’ he wrote. The CIA has been in touch with at least some Americans engaging in projects on the island, but those discussions are largely preliminary and predate the Rubio post, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN. It is unclear if the bold message from Rubio will drive more Cubans to engage with CIA in efforts to oust the island’s communist government, but the agency itself sent out a video in Spanish, moments after Rubio’s tweet, with step-by-step directions on how to securely contact the US spy agency. President Donald Trump, speaking on the midterm campaign trail, has said that the US would deal with Cuba on the “way back from Iran.” “We’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran. We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said to a South Florida midterm rally crowd, repeating a claim he’s made several times. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships. We’ll pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the game.” CNN’s Kylie Atwood contributed reporting.

title: New polls have more good news for Democrats’ Senate hopes
content: New surveys confirm just how much Democrats have expanded the Senate map in the 2026 midterm elections. The New York Times/Siena polls — the first high-quality surveys in some states — show Democrats with a bona fide pickup opportunity in South Carolina and possibly another one in Florida. The Minnesota survey, meanwhile, suggests that GOP hopes of an unlikely pickup there might have been dashed. One poll in a given state should not be oversold. (And despite Democratic momentum, many races this year are within the margin of error .) But given the dearth of polling in these three particular states — and the stakes of each race this year — the new surveys are worth delving into. The big news is that appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews are tied at 48% among likely voters in South Carolina. It’s the first high-quality public poll of the state, and it suggests the race is not just potentially winnable for Democrats, but something of a toss-up, which is astounding in a state President Donald Trump won by 18 points in 2024. It comes after another Times/Siena poll showed a dead heat in Kansas — a state Trump won by 16 points. And it’s clear why the South Carolina race is close: Republicans nominated a Trump-picked candidate with major qualification questions looming over her. While likely voters said by 13 points that Andrews (who is a physician) has the “right experience to be an effective senator,” they say by 7 points that Graham (the previously largely unknown sister of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham) does not . Among independents, 59% say Andrews has the right experience, while just 31% say Graham does. While 62% of Democrats strongly agree that Andrews has the right experience, only 35% of Republicans strongly agree that Graham does. That’s a brutal assessment from Graham’s own party. All of which helps explain why Andrews leads 57%-37% among independents and even pulls 7% of Republican likely voters. The data also suggests that GOP attempts to paint Andrews as an extremist — largely by invoking her past comments on transgender rights and using an anti-transgender slur against her — have so far fallen flat. Just 39% of likely voters in this conservative state say she’s too far to the left. There’s not yet high-quality polling in some other red states where the GOP could be feeling nervous — like Nebraska and even Mississippi, where Trump appeared on Monday. But the Times/Siena polls in Kansas and South Carolina show that Democrats have lots of opportunities. Another big finding was a poll suggesting Democrats don’t have too much to worry about in Minnesota. Up until now, the limited evidence had suggested the state, which backed Kamala Harris by 4 points, was something of a Democratic headache . The New York Times/Siena survey shows Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan leading Republican former TV sportscaster Michele Tafoya 54%-40% . The poll does suggest voters have real concerns about Flanagan being too far to the left, with even 17% of her own supporters saying that about her. She’s barely winning any GOP votes — unlike many other Democratic Senate candidates . And she’s not especially popular. But the poll suggests the electorate could just be too friendly to Democrats for any of that to matter. Democrats lead by 18 points on the generic ballot in the state, and 57% of likely voters have a strongly unfavorable view of Trump. Even if the Minnesota electorate doesn’t wind up being quite as blue as that, Tafoya would seem to face an uphill battle in what looks like a good Democratic year. Flanagan even leads by double digits — 54%-39% — among independents. A third survey seems to confirm that Florida — which has trended quite Republican in the Trump era — is a second-tier target for Democrats. The poll shows GOP Sen. Ashley Moody leading Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon by 6 points, 50-44% . It follows a University of North Florida poll last week that put Moody up by a similar 4-point margin, 49%-45% . Republicans will be happy their lead remains outside the margin of error. But that’s still competitive. Despite this state being widely written off when Democrats nominated Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, just 37% of likely voters say she’s too far to the left. And Nixon leads 52%-38% among independents. It would seem difficult for Nixon to get over the hump in a state that has trended so Republican. But at the very least, the New York Times/Siena poll suggests the governor’s race is in play. It shows GOP Rep. Byron Donalds at 48% and Democratic former Rep. David Jolly at 44% — a 4-point margin that is very close to the poll’s 3.9-point margin of error. Even losing the governor’s race in Florida would be a major GOP setback.

title: Democrats were reportedly behind the other Dan Sullivan. Here’s what it could mean
content: An October surprise has surfaced in a race that could well determine who wins the Senate majority in next week’s midterm elections. An investigation by the New York Times confirms something that’s been widely suspected but never proven: that Democrats were behind a potential spoiler candidate in Alaska — the other Dan Sullivan — who qualified for the general election ballot. There are plenty of reasons why this may or may not ultimately matter in the Alaska Senate race. But perhaps more striking is the question of why Democrats would think putting up such a candidate was a risk worth taking in the first place, given how little potential payoff it gives them. First, the details of the Times story. Staffers and lawyers for Democratic nominee Mary Peltola and other operatives aligned with the campaign spent months recruiting candidates they hoped could take votes away from GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, the newspaper reported. That effort included finding people who shared the senator’s name. Eventually, they were able to get Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. into the race, and he qualified for the ranked-choice general election by finishing in the top four in the August primary. Among those confirming the story is Peltola’s former campaign manager and longtime aide, who was fired in August during an overhaul of the campaign. Elisa Rios said Peltola herself wasn’t directly involved but was “definitely aware.” The reporting contradicts previous denials of any role in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. by the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — neither of which responded to the Times’ questions but again denied involvement. The DSCC similarly told CNN that it is “not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.” The Peltola campaign did not immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment. From a moral standpoint, the story is pretty damning. Not only could the whole effort credibly be called an attempt to deceive voters, but the new reporting sharply undercuts Democrats’ previous — and ongoing — denials. To be sure, it’s hardly the first time something like this has happened in politics — it’s become a fairly popular tactic these days to meddle in the other side’s primary in hopes that it will nominate a less-electable candidate. A GOP-aligned super PAC this cycle has also spent money to promote a socialist third-party candidate in the Ohio Senate race. Alaska’s ranked-choice system has also quickly devolved into efforts to ensure the third and fourth candidates who make the general election ballot share party affiliations with opponents. Outside groups have spent significant sums to elevate complete political unknowns — including a man running as a Democrat who is currently serving in prison and who has never been to Alaska, whom Republicans have promoted. But it’s one thing to try to influence voters’ existing choices in a misleading way; it’s another to try to directly plant a candidate whose purpose is to confuse voters. And it’s rare to see that traced directly to the campaign that’s reportedly behind it. It’s understandable if Alaska voters resent that. The flipside of that argument is that this perception might already be baked-in — that voters already assumed Democrats were behind it. Perhaps they’re just used to it all by now, given how much gamesmanship there has been with the state’s ranked-choice system. Peltola has also already dealt with some very tough headlines in the race. That includes both the August staff shake-up right before the primary, and also another Times investigation centered on staff accusing her of angry and profane outbursts that included slurs for gay people and people with intellectual disabilities. (Peltola’s campaign cited her grieving over the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023, and GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski at the time vouched for Peltola .) Those news cycles didn’t seem to cost Peltola. A New York Times/Siena poll a month ago showed her leading Sen. Sullivan among likely voters by 7 points — similar to the 8 points she led Sullivan by on primary day. That poll also showed voters still liked Peltola 50%-42%, even after the negative coverage. Those margins are also important here. While it’s still unclear who will vote in the general election and Alaska is generally viewed as a tossup, Peltola’s leads in that poll and on primary day have been significant. They suggest she might be able to withstand it even if some voters suddenly balk at her. And finally, there’s the fact that lots of voters have simply … already voted. Nearly 60,000 people had already voted early or absentee as of early this week. That’s more than one-fifth of the total turnout in recent midterm elections. Regardless, the new report is a stain on Peltola’s candidacy. And what’s particularly remarkable about it is how unlikely the other Dan Sullivan’s candidacy ever was to matter. As I wrote back in August , it was unlikely Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. would ever take enough voters from Sen. Dan Sullivan to truly make the difference. That’s in large part because the state’s ranked-choice system allows anybody who is confused to rank both of them, and have their vote eventually count for the senator. For Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to matter, people would have to vote for him and “exhaust” their ballot without also voting for Sen. Dan Sullivan — or rank the senator behind Peltola. Some voters might do that. But Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. took few votes in the primary (2.5%), and many of his voters appeared to be Peltola supporters who wanted him in the general election. The general election would have to be exceedingly close for him to make the difference. Also: Sen. Dan Sullivan is the only one listed on the ballot as a Republican and as the incumbent. Because of all of that, the new revelations could now wind up hurting Peltola more than the other Sullivan’s candidacy helps — even if it doesn’t push things too far either way. And you can bet you’ll hear plenty about it from President Donald Trump, whose Justice Department is already seeking to elevate this issue with a rather dubious lawsuit . Trump needs no invitation (or actual evidence) to accuse Democrats of cheating. The Democrats have given him something to work with here.

title: Inside the Trump administration’s controversial lists of alleged noncitizen voters
content: In the closing days of the midterms, the Trump administration has sent multiple states lists of what it alleges are noncitizens on the voter rolls, intensifying its controversial efforts to stop those people from voting in the election. In California, the administration claimed there were 20,000 people who could be noncitizens on the rolls, while in Washington state, the administration alleged this week that 400 possible noncitizen voters had voted 1,500 times in past elections. The Justice Department sent letters to both states demanding they set aside the ballots of those the department claimed could be noncitizens — and sued California when the state said that the request ran afoul of its laws. The demands this month of California and Washington marked a significant escalation of the administration’s efforts to hunt voter fraud by creating lists of potential noncitizen voters, one of numerous ways the federal government has tried to prove President Donald Trump’s baseless claims of mass voter fraud. The allegations have sparked questions about how the administration created its lists of voters who could be noncitizens — and criticism that its claims of tens of thousands of noncitizens voters have whittled down under scrutiny. State election officials and election experts have questioned the validity of the data the Trump administration is relying on to make its sweeping allegations — in addition to the decision to bring these demands to the states as early voting in the midterm election is already underway. At a district court hearing Tuesday in the California case, attorneys for the secretary of state, Los Angeles County and outside groups argued that the federal government’s data was outdated, flawed and was a “recipe for disenfranchisement” of US citizens. “This is a deeply troubling process, that is trying to use social security numbers that they’ve glued to the voter file, to go fishing for anyone who has an alien number,” said Anna Baldwin, an attorney arguing on behalf of the League of United Latin American Citizens and NAACP. Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, argued that the federal government had “developed credible evidence” of noncitizens on the rolls that California refused to address. Essayli argued that the federal government was trying to “protect votes of lawful citizens.” While much of the case focused on whether the federal government could preempt state election law when the Constitution primarily gives the power to administer elections to the states, the circumstances surrounding how the government came up with the lists of voters were also a frequent point of contention. Essayli offered to have the DHS officials who submitted sworn statements testify at Tuesday’s hearing to help explain the process that was used to determine the voters on the list were not citizens. Instead, US District Judge David Carter, a Clinton appointee, said he’s appointing a special master to dig into the data provided by both the federal government and Los Angeles County, ahead of the state’s December 3 deadline to cure ballots. Ahead of Tuesday’s hearing, a three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit US Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department’s California lawsuit on Monday in a 2-1 decision on procedural grounds. But the two judges who sided with the state, Trump appointee Mark Bennett and Biden appointee Gabriel Sanchez, both wrote in concurring opinions they also would have ruled against DOJ. In his opinion, Sanchez wrote that California and LA County “have expressed serious doubts about the accuracy and reliability of the United States’ data and methodology used to generate this list and contend that this extraordinary request threatens to disenfranchise thousands of California voters.” He asked several pointed questions during Sunday’s emergency hearing about the data and list the Justice Department was using to make its claims and how the Trump administration arrived at its conclusions. “Your claims very much depend on the reliability of that list,” Sanchez said to DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly. The Trump administration has claimed even larger numbers of noncitizens on state voter rolls. After Trump’s July primetime speech on election fraud, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed there were more than 190,000 voters registered in California who “may be” noncitizens. California was one of several Democratic-run states that Mullin singled out after Trump’s speech. “We’ve identified 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in just four states,” Mullin told reporters, citing findings in California, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Nevada. While Mullin stated the figures as facts, those numbers have shrunk considerably under scrutiny in the months since. In Nevada, for instance, DHS alleged it had identified 15,903 noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. But in a follow-up meeting, DHS officials told the state they had “confirmed” just 185 Nevada registrants as noncitizens through manual review. Nevada election officials pushed back. “As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens. You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise,” a Nevada official wrote to DHS last month. Donnelly, the DOJ attorney, disputed this at Sunday’s hearing, however, saying that Nevada’s leaders were basing this solely on voters attesting they were citizens when they registered. “That, candidly, we do not think constitutes proof that our list was invalid,” he said. Asked about the downward shift in California from 190,000 voters to the 20,000 now being alleged, Donnelly said during Sunday’s hearing that the lower number was the result of further checks by DHS. After a review of more than 100 million voter records across both Democratic- and Republican led states, DHS is still claiming it has found 300,000 “potential” noncitizens. As of mid-September, the agency had opened 1,620 investigations based on the review, and so far, the effort has led to around 160 arrests. During Tuesday’s court hearing, Carter told Essayli that the government already had a way to handle noncitizens who voted. “You’ve got a remedy for goodness sakes, go out and indict,” the judge said incredulously. A DHS spokesperson said in a statement that “190,000 remains the number of potential noncitizens registered to vote in California that DHS asked Secretary (of State Shirley) Weber to review.” “The 20,000 referenced by DOJ is a subset of registrants that have gone through the manual verification process so far,” the spokesperson said, adding that the DHS process was a “commonsense step to secure our elections.” DHS has been vague in correspondence to states about how it came up with its lists of voters it believes are noncitizens, but more details have emerged in the California lawsuit. USCIS and Homeland Security investigations officials have said in court filings they obtained California’s public voter list in August 2025. While the voter list was obtained from the secretary of state’s office, DOJ redacted who specifically obtained it from the state. The Trump administration “was supplied a list that was purchased” from California, Donnelly said during Sunday’s hearing. Earlier this year, DHS began analyzing the file, and it used a third-party system to further analyze the data and compare it to DHS immigration databases to identify potential noncitizens. Then, DHS officials say they checked the findings against federal databases and conducted manual checks of voter files. “These processes resulted here in a culled list of people who are likely to be noncitizens and who registered to vote in the upcoming 2026 federal election,” wrote Nicolas Bartell, associated director of Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate at USCIS. Wren Orey, managing director of the Bipartisan Policy Center’s Elections Project, said the third-party information appeared to be used to “backfill personally identifiable information based on the information on the publicly available voter list.” “That seems to me like a big risk that they were getting high rates of false positive matches,” Orey said. While Donnelly said he did not know the third parties used during Sunday’s 9th Circuit hearing, Bartell wrote in his declaration this week that USCIS “enhances” the voter roll data through Lexis Nexis’ Accurint, a commercial data company. In a whistleblower report filed with Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California, the whistleblower alleged that certain information not included in the source data was brought in through a process referred to as “supplemental magic.” DOJ is relying on a voter list in California that’s publicly available, because the state rejected the Justice Department’s attempt to obtain its unredacted voter file, which would contain sensitive information like Social Security numbers. DOJ has sought unredacted voter lists from nearly every state and has sued roughly 30 states that refused to turn them over but has lost every court decision on the matter so far. Christina McCall, an attorney for the state, argued that the government’s explanation doesn’t sufficiently spell out the way that the administration compiled its data — or how it even obtained the state’s voter rolls. “They’re not reliable, they’re vague, and they lack personal knowledge,” she said of the state’s lists of alleged noncitizen voters. Bartell stated in his declaration that USCIS compares the data it compiles against databases from the State Department and Social Security Administration to weed out US citizens on its lists who have a passport, confirming they’re citizens, or have died. The immigration agency then assigns a “confidence level” for each possible noncitizen match, followed by a manual review. Those cases are then referred to HSI for further investigation. In separate litigation, which led to a federal court last week ordering DHS to stop certain investigative actions in its hunt for noncitizen voters, DOJ attorney Kelsey Helland argued that the groups suing did not have evidence that US citizens were impacted by the steps DHS took going from large list of suspected noncitizen voters to a smaller list of individuals who are investigated. “That’s the initial step, and it goes through various sources of cross-checking databases, and there’s safeguards where USCIS officers are instructed not to keep going if it appears that a person is a citizen,” Helland said during a District Court hearing last week. In that litigation, a redacted HSI official touched on the potential inaccuracies in the agency’s data. “When potential inaccuracies were identified in the USCIS lists, DHS sought further resources to prevent inaccuracies and developed a new model for generating leads for HSI’s unlawful voting investigations,” the official wrote. Over the past year, DHS has also sought to identify noncitizens on voter rolls through its Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements database — known as “SAVE” — particularly in states that voluntarily turned over their unredacted voter files. The Supreme Court allowed the federal government to continue using SAVE for its investigations last month, but DHS said that the database was not used to compile the list it sent California. Election experts say that it’s still not clear how reliable the DHS matches may be, especially given that the Trump administration is using a publicly available voter file, not the state’s list that contains personally identifying information like Social Security numbers. “We still don’t have all the information about what kinds of databases are used. And then more to the point, what level of matching is sufficient,” said Derek Muller, an election law professor at Notre Dame Law School. California has argued in court filings that the DHS voter file used to compile the list of 20,000 voters it believes could be noncitizens is based on data more than a year old and could be subject to false positives. “The Executive’s own declarations describe a bulk data match that began with a voter roster more than a year old, obtained from an unidentified source, supplemented through an unnamed commercial platform, and compared against federal databases,” Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan wrote in a factual declaration for the case. “Other states’ experience confirms why such matches require investigation and individualized proof,” Logan added. Logan’s office took a sample of 200 voters from the 7,035 names with LA County addresses. His office found that of the 200 individuals, 42.9% had canceled voter registration records and 4.6% were considered inactive, meaning they were not mailed ballots this year, Aman Bhullar, an assistant registrar/recorder who works on IT and technology, wrote in a declaration. Bhullar said that more than 71% of the sample had never voted, and 38.9% of those who had a birthplace reported indicated they were born in the US. In Washington state, which received the letter from the Justice Department Tuesday, the secretary of state’s office noted that one of the 400 records was from 1994. “The system the DOJ uses frequently flags legitimate U.S. citizens as noncitizens, jeopardizing their legal right to vote,” the secretary of state’s office said in a statement. In a new court filing this week, DHS officials pushed back on California’s sample of 200 voters. Bartell wrote in a declaration that UCSIS reviewed 51 voters on the DHS list “where California’s voter roll indicates the person claimed to be born in the United States.” “After a thorough review of the immigration records of all the individuals on the County’s Sample List, it was determined that none of the individuals USCIS matched to the County’s Sample List were born in the United States according to USCIS records,” Bartell wrote, though he acknowledged four of the voters “might have a claim to U.S. citizenship,” even though they weren’t born in the United States.

title: Tory Brexit was ‘harder’ than promised in EU referendum, says Andy Burnham
content: Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum. In another series of announcements connected to his plan to seek closer links with the EU, Burnham told ministers at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that the current deal was a bad one, before writing to frontbenchers setting out his hopes to address this. Brexit was also the main subject of Burnham’s exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, with the prime minister saying the UK had been “paralysed” by the lack of a Conservative plan after the vote. A Downing Street summary of the cabinet meeting put his comments about Brexit above even those concerning the budget, which the chancellor, John Healey, was to deliver soon afterwards. “The prime minister opened by setting out how he would shortly write to cabinet on the UK’s relationship with the EU,” it said, adding: “He said the Brexit deal left by the last government had been bad for the UK and had led to a harder Brexit than had been promised at the referendum.” The letter to ministers made similar points, and ended with a warning from Burnham that they should not express opinions about the future shape of relations with the EU before a review of longer-term options. “It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period,” he said. “It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.” It follows reports that some ministers , including Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, have worries about the idea of a revised deal potentially bringing back the free movement of people to and from the EU, something Burnham has talked up as a possibility. The letter set out Burnham’s two-stage approach to reforming Brexit, beginning with any initial changes that will stay within Labour’s 2024 manifesto – which committed to remaining outside the EU’s customs union and single market, and not reinstating freedom of movement – a process that will formally kick off when the prime minister attends a European summit next month. Anything more substantial would need to wait until after the next election, with Burnham saying he wanted a discussion on what this might entail. “I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain,” he said in the letter. “It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration. It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum. Beyond it, we will need to consider the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan. I will set out the next steps for this process around the summit. “Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.” Any fundamental changes in the relationship “would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament”, he wrote, adding: “This is government policy to which cabinet collective responsibility applies.” Challenged by Badenoch at PMQs about his Brexit plans, Burnham reiterated his criticism of the current deal, saying the UK “was paralysed by the party opposite” in the wake of the referendum. In response, Badenoch said that Burnham had been using freedoms allowed under Brexit, for example, the ability to remove VAT from energy bills: “What he should be saying is: ‘Thank you.’”
